Immigration au Québec : quand les mythes: Immigration in Quebec: When Myths Meet Lived Realities
Les discours sur l’immigration se durcis: Rhetoric about immigration is hardening and shaping a perception that contrasts with reality. A new tool aims to set the record straight.
J’ai assisté, le jeudi 4 décembre, à la: On Thursday, December 4, I attended an evening at Café les Oubliettes on myths about immigration. That is where I heard the testimonies of Dounia*, as well as several participants and young people in the room.
Pour comprendre certains enjeux liés aux: To understand some of the issues tied to precarious status, I also did a phone interview with Adam*, a temporary worker living outside the major urban centres. Finally, I interviewed Amel Zaazaa, director of the Observatoire pour la justice migrante, to better understand the method and sources used in the kit presented at the event.
Cet article s’appuie donc sur ces rencon: This article is therefore based on those conversations, on the public discussions held during the evening, and on the data and research cited during the discussion.
<strong>Est-ce que le Québec accueille t: Does Quebec take in too many immigrants? Are asylum seekers overwhelming public services? Is the housing crisis linked to the arrival of foreign nationals? Are temporary workers a burden? These questions, fuelled by political and media discourse, now dominate public debate. In this climate, the Observatoire pour la justice migrante (OPLJM) and Amnistie internationale Canada francophone presented a popular education kit on December 4 called “Brisons les mythes” (“Breaking the Myths”), meant to equip the public to face preconceived ideas about immigration. It is a tool grounded in data, but also in testimonies and lived experiences.
Quand Dounia* prend la parole, un silenc: When Dounia* speaks, a hushed silence falls over the room at Café les Oubliettes. Her voice hesitant but her gaze proud, the small woman with short hair asks the question that has haunted her since she arrived in Quebec: “What does it mean, a woman without status?” she asks. In the room, the chairs stop moving. “Because we’re always seen as illegal people.”
Dounia has lived in Montréal for years. She has no work permit, no health insurance card, and no official right to study or to declare herself a resident. “But none of that makes me a criminal,” she insists. Like her, many people came to Canada on a visitor visa, others on a temporary permit: they studied, worked or filed an asylum claim. Then a refusal, an expired visa, an employer who didn’t complete the necessary steps, a divorce, an administrative error or simply delays (sometimes of several years) turned their lives upside down.
Elle raconte les frontières traversées,: She talks about the borders crossed, the things given up and the losses. “You leave a country because you’re looking for safety, hope, or just a chance to live.” But once here, she says, you become “an incomplete file, a refusal, a non-compliant case.”
Dounia souffre de l’idée voulant que les: Dounia is pained by the idea that people without status are illegal. “No woman becomes status-less by choice. It’s always a flight that was forced on her,” she says. The room listens, motionless. “Being without status means living in a country without having the right to. No right to officially exist, no right to be sick, no right to study.” The words fall one by one. She speaks of a “real but denied existence,” of a life shaped by fear: fear of a knock at the door, fear of an ID check, fear of losing your child or your home. “Fear becomes a second skin.”
Puis, elle évoque ce qu’on ne voit jamai: Then she brings up what is never seen: the houses cleaned, the children looked after, the restaurant kitchens, the care given to seniors. “This country runs because of us. But our presence is written down nowhere. We are indispensable, and yet invisible.”
Lorsque Dounia conclut en déclarant que: When Dounia concludes by declaring that “the absence of papers must never mean the absence of rights,” the room reacts almost as one. The applause lasts a long time. She lowers her eyes slightly, moved. “We’re not asking for a privilege,” she says. “We’re asking for the right to exist without fear.”
<strong>« Un travailleur temporaire ne c: “A temporary worker can only count on himself”
Adam* est arrivé au Québec en 2023. Info: Adam* arrived in Quebec in 2023. A computer scientist by training, specializing in inventory management and ERP systems, he had been recruited from abroad by a Montréal logistics company. The promised contract: 24 months, with the possibility of obtaining permanent residence after two years of work – a prospect confirmed by the international recruitment agency that was assisting him.
À son arrivée à Montréal, il découvre to: Upon arriving in Montréal, however, he discovered a closed work permit valid for only 12 months. “I quit a stable job in Algeria for a two-year contract here, certainly not to end up with a one-year permit,” he says. His wife and three children, whom he hasn’t seen in three years, are waiting for him on the other side of the migration project.
Entre démarches administratives, renouve: Through administrative procedures, permit renewals (with delays of 6 to 12 months) and a dispute with his first employer settled before the CNESST, he managed to convert his closed permit into an open one.
Comme travailleur temporaire, Adam fait: As a temporary worker, Adam is part of the group of immigrants often singled out by the government as being behind the decline of French, the lack of affordable housing and even homelessness. “Hearing that we’re responsible for what’s going wrong here breaks my heart,” he confides.
La réalité de ce travailleur qualifié es: The reality of this skilled worker, however, is far from the picture conveyed by some political discourse. Living outside the major urban centres and employed by a multinational, he pays his taxes, his rent and his daily expenses “like everyone else.” Yet he has no access to the RAMQ or to any social assistance. “A temporary worker can only count on himself,” he points out.
À la lumière de son parcours, il est dif: In light of his story, it is hard to argue that temporary immigrants are a burden. This myth, addressed in the kit, is also challenged by the many cases of <l1>French-speaking, skilled workers revealed during the recent outcry against the cancellation of the PEQ</l1>.
Au Café les Oubliettes, les témoignages: At Café les Oubliettes, the testimonies have a real effect: first a dense silence, then a series of interventions that broaden the debate. Several participants describe their daily lives in schools, where the political climate often walks in through the classroom door.
Une mère de Saint-Michel, qui a deux ado: A mother from Saint-Michel, who has two teenage daughters in high school, describes “the backsliding of discussions” on the rights of immigrants and the absence of tools to discuss these subjects calmly. “Sometimes they come home and tell me what’s being said in class… and it’s unimaginable,” she says, mentioning along the way “a necessary educational effort” to create spaces where young people can ask their questions without judgment.
Une autre intervenante parle de l’inconf: Another speaker talks about the discomfort of teachers, caught in an institutional framework that is “increasingly tense,” and sometimes hesitant to use new teaching tools. One participant reminds the room that “you can’t deconstruct anything in fear and guilt,” adding that making concepts clear and accessible, particularly regarding the rights of immigrants, would allow teachers to play their role fully.
Une troisième voix parle d’asymétrie de: A third voice speaks of an information asymmetry. She describes the challenge of navigating between political announcements, media positions and students’ reactions: “They tell me: ‘I agree with you, but that’s not what they tell me on TV.’” For her, getting through this fog of information takes collective work: “We can’t do it if we’re not together.”
Enfin, une travailleuse communautaire ré: Finally, a community worker sums up the feeling that seems to run through the room: the importance of not leaving the people directly affected to face these changes alone. “We all have a responsibility not to look away,” she says, insisting on the need to open conversations and to remind those concerned “that they’re not alone.” For her, the stakes are emotional too: “While the statistics scroll by, people are left shaken.”
<strong>La crise du logement n’est pas i: The housing crisis is not caused by immigration
C’est sans doute l’idée la plus répandue: It is arguably the most widespread idea in current political discourse: if rents are skyrocketing, it must first of all be the fault of “temporary immigration.”
La trousse « Brisons les mythes » confir: The “Brisons les mythes” kit confirms what the Front d’action populaire en réaménagement urbain (FRAPRU) and many housing rights organizations keep repeating: the housing crisis in Quebec is not caused by immigration. Together with this national housing rights coalition, it points to other known factors unrelated to immigration: luxury condos have multiplied, while social housing has not been funded to the level of need.
En tout cas, « le temps d’attente pour u: In any case, “the waiting time for low-rent housing (HLM) in Quebec would not be shortened by restricting [immigrants] with precarious status, since [they] are not eligible for it,” FRAPRU adds. On top of that come the growing presence of Airbnb, real estate speculation, the increase in secondary residences outside the major urban centres and the shortage of seniors’ residences. According to the Institut de recherche et d’informations socio-économiques (IRIS), the housing crisis has been worsening for nearly 20 years, well before the recent rise in immigration.
Lors du débat, un intervenant rappelle q: During the discussion, one speaker points out that thousands of temporary agricultural workers from South America are housed directly by the farms that employ them: “So these people don’t count in the housing crisis. But unfortunately, M<sup>s</sup>. Duranceau (minister responsible for Government Administration and the Efficiency of the State, editor’s note) keeps trying to lump them all together.”
Le secteur de la construction lui-même d: The construction sector itself depends on immigrant labour to build the housing that is lacking. “A bit more and they’ll ask them to go back to their own countries, but to build our housing remotely,” quips comedian <l1>Emna Achour in a video devoted to this myth</l1>.

La directice de l'’Observatoire pour la: The director of the Observatoire pour la justice migrante, Amel Zaazaa, researcher Sadjo Paquita and campaigns manager of Amnistie internationale Canada francophone, Marisa Berry Méndez. Photo: Mégane Dorsaz
Pour Amel Zaazaa, directrice de l’Observ: For Amel Zaazaa, director of the Observatoire, the kit grew out of an observation: “Immigration has become a political Swiss Army knife. Before building an alternative discourse, we needed tools to take apart the one that was taking hold.”
Certes, dit-elle, les données sur l’immi: Data on immigration is abundant, she says, but rarely explained to the general public. Hence the need to make information and research accessible to a wider audience “so that our society can be better informed on these issues, which are very polarized. Especially in a context where there is so much false information.”
Dans la foulée de la campagne<l1> « On s: In the wake of the <l1>“On s’fera pas porter l’chapeau” campaign,</l1> the team condensed analyses, verified data and presented this new content in an accessible form, paying particular attention to young people. “We don’t tell people what to think. We give them the means to check,” she sums up.
<strong>Quand la parole revient aux jeun: When young people get the floor back
Au-delà des données, c’est la voix des j: Beyond the data, it is the voices of young people that remind us of the human scope of the debate. Mayaline, a 3<sup>rd</sup>-year high school student, stands up to read a text describing what many children of migrants experience: a public discourse that blames newcomers while exploiting them.
Les personnes immigrantes, écrit-elle, s: Immigrants, she writes, are often the “silent but essential cogs” of a Quebec that nonetheless struggles to recognize them.
Ses mots font écho à ce que relevait plu: Her words echo what Marisa Berry Méndez of Amnistie internationale Canada francophone (co-producer of the tool) noted earlier, when she mentioned Brandolini’s law. This principle – that it takes far more energy to refute false information than to produce and spread it – sheds light on the role of popular education: slow, often quiet work, but indispensable.
